drills.q: Why did the simulator reject a loop before this unit?
options: With no clock, a value that depends on its own present value is not a
Loops always oscillate in real hardware
The simulator cannot represent them
Loops are legal but slow
drills.why: The circuit is not wrong so much as incomplete. What it is missing is a way to say when, and that is the whole subject of this unit.

drills.q: What is the rule for a D flip-flop?
options: Its output this cycle is its input from the previous cycle
Its output follows its input while the clock is high
It stores whichever input was last to change
It inverts its input once per cycle
drills.why: That single rule is all a flip-flop is here. Following the input while the enable is high describes a latch, which is a different part with a different failure mode.

drills.q: Why is the flip-flop taken as an axiom rather than built from NAND?
options: It is a pedagogical choice: real ones are built from gates with feedback,
It cannot be built from NAND
It needs analogue behaviour
It is built into the simulator for speed
drills.why: nand2tetris says so plainly, and this handbook does the same. Part III builds one properly from the standard cells a synthesiser actually uses.

drills.q: Why is a flip-flop with its output tied to its input an invalid design?
options: It holds a value and there is no way to ever load a different one
It oscillates
The output fights the input
It works, but only for one cycle
drills.why: nand2tetris labels that figure "invalid design" for exactly this reason, and it is the most valuable diagram in the book.

drills.q: What makes a register out of a flip-flop?
options: A multiplexer in the loop, whose select input is the load signal
A second flip-flop
An enable input on the flip-flop itself
A latch in front of it
drills.why: There is no separate loading mechanism anywhere in any machine. There is a multiplexer in a loop, and its select bit is what load means.

options: A time unit, saying when results are allowed to be believed
The thing that makes the computer run
A signal that triggers each gate in turn
A counter of instructions
drills.why: Everything is computing continuously whether or not a clock runs. The clock decides when it has settled enough to be trusted.

drills.q: Does a faster clock make the logic faster?
options: No. The cycle must be long enough for the slowest path, so every
Yes, gates switch faster at higher clock rates
Yes, but only for sequential logic
Only if the supply voltage rises with it
drills.why: If anything the clock makes things slower, because a fast operation still waits for the boundary. Choosing the period is choosing how much settling you are willing to wait out.

drills.q: Halfway through a cycle, an adder's output is:
options: Allowed to be garbage, and usually is while the carry ripples
Guaranteed correct
Held at its previous value
Undefined only if the inputs changed
drills.why: The design is correct if it has settled by the cycle boundary, and what happened before that does not matter. A clock cycle is a contract about when signals are allowed to be wrong.

drills.q: In a chain of flip-flops, what does the second one capture at the edge?
options: What the first one held before the edge
What the first one becomes after the edge
Whichever arrives first
It depends on propagation delay
drills.why: Every flop reads old values and writes new ones, and nothing can observe the intermediate state. That is why a chain shifts rather than collapsing to one value.

drills.q: What language feature exists to model that reading-before-writing?
options: Non-blocking assignment in Verilog
The sensitivity list
The reset clause
Continuous assignment
drills.why: Getting it wrong is the most common bug in hardware description languages, and Part III meets it as a language problem after you have met it here as a circuit property.

drills.q: How does a latch differ from a flip-flop?
options: A latch is transparent while its enable is high; a flip-flop samples at
A latch stores two bits
A latch cannot be reset
There is no difference in behaviour, only in size
drills.why: Put a latch in a loop with its enable high and the value races round as fast as the gates allow, many times within one pulse, and where it stops depends on propagation delays.

drills.q: How is edge triggering actually built?
options: Two latches in series with opposite enables, so no path is ever open all
A very short enable pulse
A comparator on the clock
An inverter chain that delays the enable
drills.why: That arrangement is called master-slave. While the first is open the second is closed, which is what turns a level into an edge.

options: An increment wired to a register
A special counting circuit
A shift register with feedback
A chain of toggles with no register
drills.why: Counting is not a new mechanism. You built the increment last unit and the register this unit, and the counter is those two connected.

drills.q: Reset on a counter is implemented as:
options: A multiplexer in front of the register, choosing zero over the computed
A special input on the flip-flop
Clearing the clock
A separate reset instruction
drills.why: And it takes priority by being the last choice made before the value is stored. That is why a processor has a reset pin rather than a reset instruction: at power-on there is no instruction to run yet.

drills.q: After rst is asserted for one cycle, the output returns to zero:
options: On the following cycle, like every other stored value
Immediately, within the same cycle
After two cycles
Only once en is also low
drills.why: Reset acts on what gets stored, and stored values appear one cycle later. Everything sequential in this unit has that same delay, and expecting otherwise is the most common way to misread a trace.
